name: Drones for Agricultural Monitoring 2: Flight Operations, Imaging and Sensors
objectives: Before every flight, run a complete pre-flight check of the aircraft, batteries, controller, settings and papers, with no checklist item skipped

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting the drone ready: the pre-flight check
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a complete pre-flight check on a drone before every flight.
This lesson builds toward: Before every flight, you will run a complete pre-flight check of the aircraft, batteries, controller, settings and papers, with no checklist item skipped.
Most drone accidents start on the ground: a cracked propeller, a half-charged battery, an out-of-date map in the app, or a compass that was not calibrated. A written checklist, used every time, prevents most of them.
Check the aircraft (frame, arms, propellers tight and undamaged, camera clean and secure), the batteries (fully charged, no swelling, contacts clean), the controller and phone or tablet (charged, app updated before you leave home, offline maps downloaded if there is no network in the field), and the settings (return-to-home height above the tallest tree or mast, home point recorded).
Do your paper check too: registration, pilot licence and any flight authorisation your authority requires for this site, carried with you or on your phone.
Step by step:
- Paper check: registration, licence, approvals for this site.
- Aircraft: frame, arms, propellers, camera.
- Batteries: charged, not swollen, clean contacts.
- Controller and phone or tablet: charged, app updated, offline maps ready.
- Settings: return-to-home height, home point, compass calibration if the app asks.
- Look around: people, animals, wind, then start.
Words to know:
- Pre-flight check: a list of checks done before every flight.
- Return-to-home (RTH): a setting that makes the drone fly back to its take-off point by itself, for example when the battery is low or the signal is lost.
- Home point: the place the drone will return to, usually where it took off.
Official sources:
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
Try it now: Write your own pre-flight checklist with at least 12 items under four headings: papers, aircraft, batteries and controller, settings. Keep it on your phone.
You can now prepare a drone with a full pre-flight check covering papers, aircraft, batteries, controller and settings.

options: The place the drone returns to by itself on return-to-home
The highest point of the farm
check.why: The home point is recorded before take-off so return-to-home flies the drone back there.

check.q: You are going to a farm with no mobile network. What do you do before you leave home?
options: Nothing; the app will work anyway
Plan to update the app in the field
Download offline maps and update the app
check.why: Apps should be updated and offline maps downloaded before you leave, because there may be no network in the field.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Flying safely within sight
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take off, fly a simple pattern and land while keeping the drone in sight.
This lesson builds toward: On a practice or approved flight, you will take off, fly a simple pattern and land while keeping the drone in sight, within the legal height limit and landing with battery to spare.
Visual line of sight (VLOS) means you, or your observer, can see the drone with your own eyes, without binoculars, the whole time. Most farm flights by smallholders and new pilots are VLOS. Flying beyond line of sight needs special approval. Nigeria's Part 21, for example, requires VLOS for smaller drones and sets a maximum height of 120 metres (400 feet) above ground for many operations; check your own country's limits.
Take off from your clear spot, climb to a safe height above trees, and hover for a few seconds to check the drone is steady. Fly slowly. Keep the drone in front of you, not overhead or behind you, so you do not lose track of which way it faces.
Watch the battery and wind. Land with enough battery left for a safe landing, never at the last percent. If the drone drifts strongly in the wind, bring it back and land.
Step by step:
- Stand at your take-off spot with your observer.
- Take off and climb above the trees; hover and check it is steady.
- Fly slowly in a square in front of you, keeping it in sight.
- Watch the battery and wind on the screen.
- Return, descend slowly and land with battery to spare.
Words to know:
- VLOS: visual line of sight: you can see the drone with your own eyes the whole flight.
- BVLOS: beyond visual line of sight: flying further than you can see; needs special approval.
- AGL: above ground level: height measured from the ground below the drone.
Official sources:
- Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA): Nig.CARs 2023 Part 21, Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems
- Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA): Unmanned Aircraft Systems
Try it now: If you have a drone and approval, fly a slow square in front of you and land with battery to spare. If not, use a free drone simulator app or watch a training video and write down the steps you saw.
You can now take off, fly a simple pattern within sight, and land safely with battery to spare.

check.q: What does keeping the drone "in front of you" help with?
options: Knowing which way the drone faces
check.why: Keeping the drone in front of you, not overhead or behind, helps you keep track of its direction.

check.q: Right after take-off the drone drifts strongly in the wind. What do you do?
options: Climb higher to escape the wind
Look away and let it fly
check.why: If the drone drifts strongly in the wind, bring it back and land.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Planning an automatic mapping flight
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a grid mapping flight with the right height, overlap and speed.
This lesson builds toward: For a field to be mapped, you will plan a grid mapping flight with height, image detail, overlap, speed and batteries, with overlap of about 70 to 80 percent forward and 60 to 70 percent to the side.
To make a map of a field, the drone flies back and forth in straight lines (a grid, sometimes called a lawnmower pattern) and takes photos that overlap. Mapping apps let you draw the field boundary, then plan the lines for you.
Height sets the detail. The higher you fly, the more ground each pixel covers and the less detail you get, but the faster you finish. The app shows this as ground sampling distance (GSD), for example 2 cm per pixel. To count maize plants you need fine detail; to see waterlogged areas, coarser is fine. Never plan above your legal height limit.
Overlap is how much each photo shares with the next. Software needs a lot of overlap to stitch photos into one map; many mapping guides suggest about 70 to 80 percent forward and 60 to 70 percent to the side, more over tall, uniform crops like maize or tea. Fly slowly enough that photos are sharp, and plan enough batteries to finish.
Step by step:
- Draw the field boundary in the mapping app.
- Choose the height: check the GSD it gives and stay under your legal limit.
- Set forward and side overlap (for example 75 and 65 percent).
- Check the flight time and number of batteries.
- Save the plan and review it again before you go to the field.
Words to know:
- Grid flight: a flight in straight back-and-forth lines that covers the whole field.
- Overlap: how much each photo shares with the next one, in percent.
- GSD: ground sampling distance: how much ground one pixel covers, such as 2 cm.
- Orthomosaic: one large, map-accurate picture stitched from many overlapping photos.
Try it now: Open a free mapping or flight-planning app (or a flight planner inside your drone's app) and draw a 2-hectare field. Try three heights and write down the GSD and flight time for each.
You can now plan a grid mapping flight and choose height, overlap and speed for the job.

check.q: What is a grid or lawnmower pattern?
options: Straight back-and-forth lines over the field
A single photo from very high
check.why: Mapping flights fly straight back-and-forth lines so the photos cover the whole field with overlap.

check.q: You want to count maize plants but your plan gives coarse detail. What do you change?
options: Fly lower for a finer GSD, within the legal limit
check.why: Flying lower gives finer detail per pixel, but never above or beyond your legal limits.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Colour (RGB) images: what you can see
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read a high-resolution colour drone image for gaps, weeds, water and damage.
This lesson builds toward: Given a high-resolution colour drone image, you will point out gaps, weeds, water, lodging and damage, and mark each spot to check on foot.
A normal colour (RGB) camera is the most useful sensor for most farms, and it comes with almost every drone. At a few centimetres per pixel you can see single maize, bean or cassava plants.
In colour images look for: gaps in rows (poor germination or plants eaten by pests), weed patches between rows, standing water and bare soil, lodged (fallen) maize or sorghum, hail or wind damage, cattle or goats in the wrong place, and blocked drains or broken fences.
Colour images can also hint at nutrient problems or disease (yellowing, uneven green), but they show it later than the eye on the ground or a multispectral camera might. Always mark the spot and check it on foot.
Step by step:
- Open the image or map and zoom out to see the whole field.
- Look for anything uneven: gaps, colour changes, water, bare soil.
- Zoom in on each one.
- Mark each spot with a number and a short note.
- Walk to the spots to check them.
Words to know:
- High-resolution image: an image with fine detail, where each pixel covers a small piece of ground.
- Lodging: when stalks of maize, sorghum or wheat bend or fall over.
Try it now: Find a drone photo or a satellite view of a farm online (or use your own). List five things you can see, mark where each one is, and say what you would check on the ground.
You can now read a colour drone image and mark gaps, weeds, water and damage to check on the ground.

check.q: In a colour image, what can a gap in a row show?
options: Poor germination or plants eaten by pests
check.why: Gaps in rows often mean seeds did not come up or plants were eaten.

check.q: The image shows an uneven, yellowish patch in a bean field. What do you do?
options: Mark the spot and check it on foot
check.why: Colour images can hint at problems, but the spot must be checked on the ground.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Multispectral and thermal sensors
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose between RGB, multispectral and thermal sensors for a farm question.
This lesson builds toward: Given a farm question, you will choose between an RGB, multispectral and thermal sensor, with a reason that fits the question and the cost.
Healthy green leaves reflect a lot of near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see. Stressed or sick leaves reflect less. A multispectral camera measures several bands of light, including near-infrared and red edge, so software can calculate vegetation indices such as NDVI that show plant vigour. FAO uses NDVI from satellites to track vegetation health across Africa; drones do the same at field scale.
A thermal camera measures surface temperature. Plants short of water close their pores and warm up, so thermal images can show water stress and blocked irrigation lines. Thermal is also good for finding animals at night or dawn.
These sensors cost more and need careful use (calibration, the right time of day). Choose them when the question needs them: early stress in a tea estate or irrigated vegetables, yes; counting gaps in a 1-acre bean plot, no, colour is enough.
Words to know:
- Near-infrared (NIR): light just beyond red that people cannot see; healthy leaves reflect a lot of it.
- Vegetation index: a number calculated from bands of light that shows how green and vigorous plants are.
- NDVI: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index: a common vegetation index from red and near-infrared light, from -1 to +1; higher usually means denser, healthier green plants.
Official sources:
- FAO GIEWS Earth Observation (NDVI and vegetation indicators)
- FAO and ITU: E-agriculture in Action: Drones for Agriculture (2018)
Try it now: For each question, choose RGB, multispectral or thermal and write why: (a) Is my drip line blocked? (b) Where did the beans not germinate? (c) Is one block of tea under stress before the leaves change colour?
You can now say what multispectral and thermal sensors show and choose the right sensor for a farm question.

check.q: What does a thermal camera measure?
check.why: A thermal camera measures surface temperature, which can show water stress.

check.q: A tea estate wants to spot stress early across its blocks. Which sensor do you suggest?
options: A thermal camera only for animals
check.why: Multispectral cameras measure near-infrared and red edge, which show plant stress earlier.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Capturing good images: light, wind and timing
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a flight so every image is sharp, evenly lit and usable.
This lesson builds toward: On the day of a mapping flight, you will set the time, light and wind limits and check every image before leaving the field, so the images are sharp, evenly lit and complete.
Images taken weeks apart can only be compared if they are taken the same way. Fly around the middle of the day, when shadows are short, and in steady light: either full sun or even cloud, not patches of cloud moving over the field. Fly at the same height and settings each time.
Wind shakes the drone and moves leaves, which blurs images and breaks stitching. Fly slower in light wind and not at all in strong wind. Make sure the lens is clean and the camera is set to focus correctly; many mapping apps set the camera for you.
For multispectral cameras, photograph the calibration panel (a card of known reflectance that comes with the sensor) before and after the flight, so software can correct for light. Before leaving the field, look through the photos: if some are blurred, dark or missing, refly that part while you are still there.
Step by step:
- Plan to fly near midday in steady light.
- Check wind; slow down in light wind, cancel in strong wind.
- Clean the lens; check camera settings.
- Multispectral: photograph the calibration panel before and after.
- Before leaving, check the photos and refly any bad section.
Words to know:
- Calibration panel: a card of known brightness photographed before and after a multispectral flight to correct for light.
- Blur: when an image is not sharp because the camera or plants moved.
Try it now: Final task: write your complete imaging flight plan for a 2-hectare maize plot: goal, sensor, height and GSD, overlap, speed, batteries, time of day, weather limits, take-off spot and checklist. If you have a drone and the required approvals, fly it and check every image before you leave.
You can now plan and capture a set of sharp, evenly lit images that can be stitched into a farm map and compared over time.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Goal and sensor No goal, or the sensor does not fit the goal. A clear goal for the flight and a sensor that fits it, with a reason. Explains why a cheaper or costlier sensor was not chosen. Height, detail and overlap Height, GSD or overlap is missing, or above the legal height limit. Height and the GSD shown by the app, forward and side overlap, speed and number of batteries. Shows how the detail fits the job, such as counting plants. Light, wind and timing No time of day or weather limits. Time of day, light, wind limits and a plan to check every image before leaving. Includes calibration panel steps or a reserve date. Pre-flight checklist The checklist misses aircraft, batteries, settings or papers. Covers aircraft, batteries, controller and app, return-to-home settings and papers. Adds the take-off spot and how the drone stays in sight. Safe flying No take-off spot, or flying beyond sight without approval. A clear take-off spot, flying within sight and the legal height, and landing with battery to spare. Names an observer and the steps if the wind rises. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

options: A card of known reflectance photographed before and after a multispectral flight
check.why: Photographing the calibration panel lets software correct for the light that day.

check.q: Patchy clouds are moving fast over the field at midday. What do you do?
options: Wait for full sun or even cloud before flying
Fly higher to get above the clouds
check.why: Steady light, either full sun or even cloud, gives evenly lit images that can be compared.
